fullPassage: Imagine you live in a small village where you and three other villagers depend on the local fish pond for food. The pond starts off with a dozen fish, and for every two fish, one baby is added each night. So, to maximize your supply of food, how many fish should you catch each day? Assume baby fish grow to full size immediately, the pond begins at full capacity, and ignore the sex of the fish. The answer? One, and not just you: every villager's food supply is maximized when each fisherman takes one fish a day. Here's the math: if each villager takes one fish, eight are left overnight. Each pair produces one baby, so the next day the pond is fully restocked with twelve. If anyone takes more than one, the number of reproductive pairs drops, and the population can't bounce back. Eventually the fish are gone and all four villagers starve. This pond is one example of a classic problem called the tragedy of the commons. It was first described in an 1833 pamphlet by economist William Forster Lloyd, on the overgrazing of cattle on village common areas. More than 100 years later, ecologist Garrett Hardin revived it to describe what happens when many individuals share a limited resource: grazing land, fishing areas, living space, even clean air. Hardin said that in these situations, people want what is good for themselves today, but that hurts everyone later. Nobody wins. We get too much grazing, too much fishing, too many people, and too much pollution. The key feature is that an individual can benefit himself while spreading the negative effects across the larger population. Let's look at our fish pond again. Each fisherman is motivated to take as many fish as he can, while any decline in reproduction is shared by the whole village. Anxious not to lose out, he concludes it's in his best interest to take an extra fish, or two, or three. But the other fishermen reach the same conclusion, and that's the tragedy. Optimizing for the self in the short term isn't optimal for anyone in the long term. The fish pond is a simple example, but the same thing really happens in the world around us. The overuse of antibiotics brought short-term gains in livestock production and in treating illnesses, but also produced antibiotic-resistant bacteria that threaten the entire population. A coal-fired power plant gives customers cheap electricity and owners profit; these local benefits help in the short term, but the pollution spreads across the entire atmosphere and lasts thousands of years. Other examples include littering, water shortages, deforestation, traffic jams, even buying bottled water. But human civilization has proven capable of something remarkable. We form social contracts, make communal agreements, elect governments, and pass laws to save our collective selves from our own individual impulses. It isn't easy, and we don't always get it right. But at our best we have shown that we can solve these problems, and can continue to if we remember Hardin's lesson: When the tragedy of the commons applies, what's good for all of us is good for each of us.

(A) Anxious not to lose out, he concludes it's in his best <u>interest</u> to take an extra fish, or two, or three.

(B) She showed great <u>interest</u> in learning how to play the violin after watching the concert last night.
questions.stem: 다음 (A), (B)의 밑줄 친 interest의 문맥적 의미로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.korean: (A)의 interest는 '이익, 이해관계' / (B)의 interest는 '흥미, 관심'
det.analysis:
❌ ① (A) 흥미 — (B) 이익: (A)(B)의 의미가 뒤바뀌어 부적절
✅ ② (A) 이익 — (B) 흥미: (A) it's in his best interest = 자신의 최선의 '이익'이다 / (B) showed great interest in learning = 배우는 데 큰 '흥미'를 보였다
❌ ③ (A) 이자 — (B) 흥미: (A)는 금융의 '이자'가 아니라 '이익/이해관계'를 뜻함
❌ ④ (A) 이익 — (B) 이자: (B)는 '이자'가 아니라 배움에 대한 '흥미'를 뜻함
det.tip: interest의 다의: ① 이익/이해관계(in his best interest) ② 흥미/관심(great interest in) ③ 이자(금융)

questions.stem:
다음 영영 정의에 해당하는 단어로 가장 적절한 것은?

"a scientist who studies the relationships between living things and their environment"

det.korean: 생물과 환경의 관계를 연구하는 과학자 → 생태학자(ecologist)
det.analysis:
❌ ① journalist — 기자. 정의와 무관
❌ ② architect — 건축가. 정의와 무관
✅ ③ ecologist — 생태학자. '생물과 환경의 관계를 연구하는 과학자'라는 정의에 정확히 부합
❌ ④ economist — 경제학자. 경제를 연구하는 사람으로, 본문의 Lloyd(economist)와 혼동을 노린 함정
det.tip: ecologist Garrett Hardin = 생태학자. economist(경제학자)와 구별 필요

questions.passage: This pond is one example of a classic problem called the tragedy of the commons. It was first __________ (describe) in an 1833 pamphlet by economist William Forster Lloyd, on the overgrazing of cattle on village common areas.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 괄호 안의 단어를 알맞은 형태로 바꿔 쓰시오. (1단어) (영어로)

det.korean: 'It was first __________'에서 be동사 뒤 수동의 의미이므로 과거분사 → described
det.analysis: 정답: described — 'It was first __________ in an 1833 pamphlet'에서 그 문제가 1833년 소책자에서 '기술되었다'는 수동의 의미. be동사(was) 뒤에는 과거분사가 오므로 describe → described. It was first described = 처음으로 기술되었다
det.tip: be동사 + 과거분사 = 수동태(~되었다). was described = 기술되었다

questions.passage: The fish pond is a simple example, but the same thing really happens in the world around us. The overuse of antibiotics brought short-term gains in livestock production and in treating illnesses, but also produced antibiotic-resistant bacteria __________ (threaten) the entire population.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 괄호 안의 단어를 알맞은 형태로 바꿔 쓰시오. (1단어) (영어로)

det.korean: 앞의 명사 bacteria를 능동으로 뒤에서 수식하는 현재분사 → threatening
det.analysis: 정답: threatening — 'produced antibiotic-resistant bacteria __________ the entire population'에서 이미 produced라는 본동사가 있으므로 threaten을 그대로 쓸 수 없다. 앞의 명사 bacteria가 개체군을 '위협하는'이라는 능동의 의미로 뒤에서 수식해야 하므로 현재분사 threatening을 쓴다. bacteria threatening the entire population = 전체 개체군을 위협하는 박테리아
det.tip: 명사 뒤에서 능동으로 수식 = 현재분사(-ing). bacteria threatening ~ = ~를 위협하는 박테리아

questions.passage: Imagine you live in a small village where you and three other villagers depend on the local fish pond for food. The pond starts off with a dozen fish, and for every two fish, one baby is added each night. So, to maximize your supply of food, how many fish should you catch each day? Assume baby fish grow to full size immediately, the pond begins at full capacity, and ignore the sex of the fish. The answer? One, and not just you: every villager's food supply is maximized when each fisherman takes one fish a day. Here's the math: if each villager takes one fish, eight are left overnight. Each pair produces one baby, so the next day the pond is fully restocked with twelve. If anyone takes more than one, the number of reproductive pairs drops, and the population can't bounce back. Eventually the fish are gone and all four villagers starve. This pond is one example of a classic problem called the tragedy of the commons. It was first described in an 1833 pamphlet by economist William Forster Lloyd, on the overgrazing of cattle on village common areas. More than 100 years later, ecologist Garrett Hardin revived it to describe what happens when many individuals share a __________: grazing land, fishing areas, living space, even clean air. Hardin said that in these situations, people want what is good for themselves today, but that hurts everyone later. Nobody wins. We get too much grazing, too much fishing, too many people, and too much pollution. The key feature is that an individual can benefit himself while spreading the negative effects across the larger population. Let's look at our fish pond again. Each fisherman is motivated to take as many fish as he can, while any decline in reproduction is shared by the whole village. Anxious not to lose out, he concludes it's in his best interest to take an extra fish, or two, or three. But the other fishermen reach the same conclusion, and that's the tragedy. Optimizing for the self in the short term isn't optimal for anyone in the long term. The fish pond is a simple example, but the same thing really happens in the world around us. The overuse of antibiotics brought short-term gains in livestock production and in treating illnesses, but also produced antibiotic-resistant bacteria that threaten the entire population. A coal-fired power plant gives customers cheap electricity and owners profit; these local benefits help in the short term, but the pollution spreads across the entire atmosphere and lasts thousands of years. Other examples include littering, water shortages, deforestation, traffic jams, even buying bottled water. But human civilization has proven capable of something remarkable. We form social contracts, make communal agreements, elect governments, and pass laws to save our collective selves from our own individual impulses. It isn't easy, and we don't always get it right. But at our best we have shown that we can solve these problems, and can continue to if we remember Hardin's lesson: When the tragedy of the commons applies, what's good for all of us is good for each of us.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 여러 개인이 함께 나눠 쓰는 것 → 한정된 자원(limited resource)
det.analysis:
❌ ① personal hobby — 개인의 취미. 여러 사람이 공유한다는 맥락과 맞지 않음
❌ ② private garden — 사적인 정원. 뒤의 '방목지, 어장, 생활 공간, 맑은 공기' 같은 공용 예시와 어울리지 않음
❌ ③ secret code — 비밀 코드. 공유 자원 맥락과 무관
✅ ④ limited resource — 한정된 자원. 'when many individuals share a __________: grazing land, fishing areas, living space, even clean air' — 여러 개인이 나눠 쓰는 한정된 자원이라는 맥락에 정확히 부합
det.tip: share a limited resource: grazing land, fishing areas... = 한정된 자원을 함께 나눠 씀

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 공동의 합의를 맺고 정부를 세우기 위해 형성하는 것 → 사회적 계약(social contracts)
det.analysis:
❌ ① personal profits — 개인의 이익. 개인의 충동에서 벗어나려는 협력 맥락과 반대
✅ ② social contracts — 사회적 계약. 'We form __________, make communal agreements, elect governments, and pass laws' — 공동의 합의를 맺고 정부를 세우며 법을 통과시키기 위해 형성하는 사회적 계약이라는 맥락에 정확히 부합
❌ ③ private fortunes — 개인의 재산. 집단적 자아를 지키려는 흐름과 반대
❌ ④ secret alliances — 비밀 동맹. 공개적으로 정부를 세우고 법을 만든다는 맥락과 어울리지 않음
det.tip: We form social contracts, make communal agreements = 사회적 계약을 맺고 공동의 합의를 함
